speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: OLD AGE PENSIONS
speechtext:
1. The old age pensions division of the department of national health and welfare employs thirteen peisons and the division of blindness control employs three persons. Other departments of the dominion government including mines and resources, trade and commerce and secretary of state are required to provide information for use of the provincial pension authorities.

LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs):	Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on March 25 I indicated that announcements of diplomatic appointments to Mexico and Australia would be made today, and I have pleasure in informing the house that Mr. Kenneth Alfred Greene, O.B.E. has been appointed as High Commissioner for Canada in Australia. Doctor Laureys in 1940 became the first High Commissioner for Canada in the Union of South Africa, where he served until 1944, when he w^as appointed Canada's first ambassador in Peru. Before entering the public service, Doctor Laureys had a distinguished academic career in the field of international economic and commercial studies.

speechtext: "Will the minister provide the committee with a statement showing the total of all bonuses, subsidies, remissions of duty, remissions of other taxes and1 other benefits, direct and indirect, which the government has paid, in order that we may have a fuller appreciation of the cost of controls? I would ask that over and above the total of these bonuses, subsidies and remissions the statement show what has been paid out each year since controls went into effect. I am sure the government has this information and can make it available. I have spent more time than I care to admit in trying to work it out for myself, and I arrived at a figure which exceeded the billion dollar mark. I then asked myself whether I was wrong in my figuring, but I have been unable to find in any report a complete statement of these payments. It would be of great assistance to the committee to have a concise statement showing exactly what these contributions by the government have been.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Some of the items would be debatable. For example, under the War Exchange Conservation Act, which was passed in December, 1940, the duties on goods imported from Great Britain in some cases were removed, in other cases they were reduced by fifty per cent and in other cases were reduced by twenty-five per cent. Undoubtedly the reduction of those duties had some effect upon the prices of the goods imported, yet those duties were not reduced or removed for the purpose of controlling prices. They were removed or reduced for another and entirely different purpose, namely,
the encouragement of imports from Great Britain so that not so many goods would be imported from the United States to the end that our stocks of hard currency would be conserved. Such items would present a problem to any one attempting to compile a complete list of tariff reductions, taxation remissions and so forth.
I do not know what should be done with subsidies which were paid for the purpose of stimulating production, or encouraging the production of high quality goods, such as certain bacon subsidies which were graded in accordance with the quality of the product, and the cheese subsidies which were graded in a similar manner. It is impossible to say whether certain subsidies were paid for the purpose of keeping prices down, for the purpose of keeping production up, or both. The main class of subsidy is that which was paid by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited, and a statement of these subsidies is to be found on page 74 of the report of the board. I shall take only a few minutes. We have seen the results of this resolution. Are we to sit here day after day, day in and day out, listening to the government trying to pacify hon. members to my left, the socialist party, the totalitarian party, and all that kind of thing? Several of them have got up and suggested that they are the same as the Labour party in England. I say that if they are, then God save Canada-when we consider what has been happening in Britain in connection with coal, electricity, power, food, and everything else.
The government of the day have at last awakened to the fact that if they are to follow the gentlemen to my left, the socialists, they are going away down deep into the sea, and they had better pause before they come to the brink-because the time is not far distant when there will be an election. They can call an election, if they want to, this year- and the sooner the better, in some ways.
We have to listen to all this kind of socialist talk. And I can tell you this, that so far as the function of the opposition in respect of this resolution is concerned, as I see it, I should have liked to see it passed on Friday night. It is not just enough to bark; to oppose is the function of an opposition. But since then a great number of extraneous matters have been brought in. Are we in the opposition going to sit here and do nothing about it? I can remember away back in March, 1939, when I asked the Minister of Justice a question along these lines. Are we going to go over the same story five or six times? That has been done here. For five or six days now we have allowed all kinds of irrelevant matters to be brought into the debate. I believe it was on April 24, 1939-it was either March or April, I am not quite sure-when I asked the former highly respected minister of justice if the War Measures Act of 1914 was still in existence. He said, "No". I said, "Yes, it is." He then looked it up, and later he found out that the War Measures Act was still in existence, that it had not been wiped off the statute books. It took a long time to declare that war at an end. That was the first matter.
I wish to stick to the text of the resolution, except to reply to one or two things which have been said. In the first place, this whole emergency measure, this War Measures Act, should have been cancelled and abrogated. The War Measures Act of 1914 has been on the statute books, with only some changes in phraseology. That is the first thing that should have been done. Then, second, I would rather see the Minister of Justice bring in separate bills for what he has left. Mind1 you, I sympathize with the minister at the present time, because he has a hard task to answer some of the questions which have been asked.
I am sorry the hon. member for Cape Breton South is not in his seat, because I was gonig to point out what Mr. Shinwell said. The Labour party over there has everything cut and dried. They are taking over the mines. Mr. Morrison said that nationalization of the mines would not in itself produce one extra truck of coal. And Mr. Attlee declared that the whole future of the Labour party depends upon the success of the nationalization of coal mines. Here are Herbert Morrison's words of December 1, 1946:
Nationalization will not in itself produce one extra truck of coal.
Unfortunately the Labour government has not thought the matter out. Mr. Shinwell admitted on June 11, 1946, that the socialist party had paid little attention to the extremely difficult technical and administrative problems which nationalization involves. Notwithstanding all that, here we have gentlemen to my left trying to persuade the government of the day and the Minister of Justice to follow them on socialism. If it does, the government will get into the sea, and it had better stop before it is too late.
I believe the resolution should have been reported before this. We would then be in position to deal with the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means. We have spent five or six days on this resolution.
I would like to have the undivided attention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He is always making speeches and taking time by raising points of order. He takes more time than anyone else and then he does not want to listen to anyone. I would like to have the attention of the minister for a moment or two. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does not like anyone to say anything that may affect his speeches. I am not in a hurry; I can wait, but I want the attention of the right hon. Minister of

Justice. The hon. member has spent enough time over there; he should go to England and join the socialist party.
I have great admiration for the minister in many ways. In 1924 I asked the Minister of Justice a question when he got up to give an opinion on a matter concerning the Toronto Hydro Electric Commission which was before the privy council and with which I had something to do on this side of the water. The minister was asked by the head of what was then called the progressives to give an opinion, and he gave that opinion. After he had spoken I called his attention to the fact that the Minister of Justice should not do what was done last Friday night. It has been a rule since confederation that the Minister of Justice, who is the Attorney General of Canada, should not be asked to give a legal opinion. I raised this question in 1924 and his predecessor said that I was right.
When the minister was asked for an opinion he gave the opinion of his deputy, Mr. Varcoe. He is an able man, and he should be because he comes from Toronto. The minister gave the substance of the opinion of the deputy minister of justice. This particular resolution will be followed by a bill and the Attorney General of Canada may be brought into the matter. The War Measures Act was brought up in the courts across the country, and no doubt this bill will be brought up for interpretation by the courts. The courts will have to find what was the intention of the legislature when they passed this bill to be based on this resolution. There may be disputes and the Attorney General of Canada or the attorney general of the provinces may be brought into the matter by order of a judge of the high court of justice or of the county court on any action to declare the new bill ultra vires. For that reason I think it wise that the Minister of Justice, who is the Attorney General of Canada should not be asked to give an opinion to the house.

Reference was made last Friday to decisions of the privy council. It is a blessing to this country that we have the privy council at the present time, otherwise everything connected with provincial rights would have been wiped out. It is the one court where the litigant can get justice and minorities their rights. You have only to read its decisions to know that that is the court that holds a system of checks and balances between federal and provincial rights under our federal system. It is a blessing to our country that we have that court.
When a war is on it is a different matter, but the war has been off for two years. The War Measures Act of 1914 should be repealed, as the hon. member for Lake Centre said the other night in his very able speech. The decisions referred to, including Snider and Toronto Electric Commissioners, do not relate to the war at all, and it is beyond me why the words "peace, order and good government" have been used as a basis for the resolution now before us. I would like to see the resolution reported. Silence in parliament, I take it, means that we are assenting to what has been done or to what has been said here for six days. A lot has been said here in the last five or six days. In my opinion the country is not going to stand much more of this socialism. The people in the constituencies are sick and tired of the increasing debt of this country and the over-taxation and over-government that we have. Lord Hals-bury, Lord Chief Justice, once said:
I think it is something new in the history of this house that it should he admitted that a bill is injurious and unjust, and that nevertheless your Lordships are not to protest against it.
The public is bewildered that no lead is given to them. On September 11, 1945, which I think was the third day after we met in this parliament, I objected to what had been provided for in the address. I said that in my opinion the country demanded certain measures for private industry and private enterprise and initiative. That is the key to the solution of our economic problems from Vancouver to Halifax. There should be an extension of the national policy, not only for capital but for labour, for coal and for all other industries. That should be the policy of the future as far as the government is concerned. I do not blame the hon. member for Vancouver Centre for getting sick and tired of all this business. He is supposed to be an astute politician and I know he is getting sick and tired of what he hears

Mr. Chairman, just for my own sake at any rate, and to keep the record straight, I should like to call your attention to what you said a few moments ago, namely that there was only one question before the house, whether we were in favour of or against controls. I very respectfully wish to differ in opinion with you, Mr. Chairman.
There are fifty-seven bills before us, all in one bill. Only ten or fifteen of them, so far as I can gather, refer to controls. The rest refer to all kinds of other matters. The objection I raised earlier in this debate, and which since the debate started I have found no reason for abandoning, is to the method followed in bringing before the house fifty-seven money bills in one bill without explaining what each money bill involves, what specific or at least what readily ascertainable amount is involved. I do not believe that is the proper way in which legislation should be introduced. It may be a more convenient way, but democracy does not look to the convenience of ministers or rules but rather to the convenience and ease of the governed.
Certain suggestions have been made to the minister bjr the member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Eglinton, the hon. member for Vancouver South and others, to the effect that it would be possible to take about twenty-five of these orders in council out of this omnibus bill and introduce and pass them separately. The only answer I have heard from the minister is that he does not wish to give priority to these particular bills. But what would prevent him, for instance, from introducing a bill to amend the Civil Service Act to give a preference in civil service appointments to returned soldiers who served in the war of 1939-1945? I am not asking for priority for that bill. If it is not passed by May 15, I for one would be quite willing to have the order in council extend until such time as that bill could be passed. But do not get that mixed up with other things that have no connection with it. I may be all wrong, but I think it is throwing doubt in the minds of these veterans as to their right to have the same sort of treatment as the soldiers of 1914-18 received by providing for it in this kind of bill. It seems to 83166-1141
me that everybody is agreed upon giving the veterans this preference. Therefore let us introduce a bill to amend the Civil Service Act accordingly and send it before a committee of this house, if you like, and if it is not passed by May 15 there will be no difficulty in granting an extension of these four orders in council. The same with respect to old age pensions and the same with respect to labour relations.
I have strong objections to having inserted in our statutes fifty-seven pieces of legislation in one bill, to be duplicated by other statutes. Look how ridiculous it will make us appear in the years to come. When people are looking over the statutes of this year of grace, 1947, they will see, in identical language, one piece of legislation appear as an appendix to an omnibus bill stating that the returned soldier of the war of 1939-45 will have certain preferences, and then twenty pages further on in the same statute book they will find a law to amend the Civil Service Act stating exactly, so far as one part of it is concerned, what is contained in an appendix to an earlier statute. It seems to me that it will only tend to involve people in confusion.
I should like to make reference to something else that has been said in the course of the debate. It seems to me that a debate on the resolution is perfectly proper. There is nothing out of order in it. I do not know of any rule of the house that would preclude members from discussing the financial provisions of any resolution. That is what the resolution is for. It seems to me it is going a little far to be repeatedly telling us we are out of order in discussing the financial provisions of the resolution that is before the committee.
The only precedent I know of, and I referred to it a week or so ago when I made a few remarks in the house, is the unemployment and farm relief bill of Mr. Bennett in 1931 and the Unemployment and Farm Relief Continuance Act of 1932. That bill was debated-I have not the exact dates but it looks to me as if it was debated from March 8 until the end of March or the beginning of April and then closure had to be applied to pass the resolution. At that time the debate was on the financial provisions of the resolution and the extraordinary powers being taken by the Bennett government. That was not so very long ago. It is the latest precedent of this kind of extraordinary legislation that I know of, and I can see no reason why there should be complaint if we try to discuss what should be discussed on a resolution introductory to a money bill.
I can see no reason why we should not ask the minister to withdraw from the appendix

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the position taken by the hon. member for Quebec South. As I understand it, one of his objections to this bill is that this is virtually blank cheque legislation and that the amount of the expenditures contemplated under these orders in council should be specified in the resolution. I want to point out that this resolution is not similar to the resolution to which mj' hon. friend referred as having been passed in 1931. The point of difference is extremely important. The resolution which related to farm and unemployment relief, and which will be found at page 4275 of Hansard of July 29, 1931, reads as follows:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemployment and farm relief; and for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada; and to authorize the governor in council to expend for the said purposes out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may from time to time be necessary.
The position we took at that time was that authority to pay undefined and unlimited sums out of the consolidated revenue fund was in effect a blank cheque which should not be given to the government. The situation is entirely different if the money is to be provided out of money appropriated by parliament, as is the case in the legislation before the committee.
The other night the hon. member referred to the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation. He pointed out the fact that one of these orders in council provided for the setting up of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation and authorized that corporation to buy and sell goods, to import goods, and to pay subsidies on goods. He argued that when we do that the minister must certainly be in a

position to come before the house and state the limits of the financial liability of the government in respect of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation. The answer to that is that the limit of our financial responsibility in respect of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation is found in the estimates. The amount voted for the proposed Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation is 135 million. That is provided for in the estimates. It will be found on page 69 of the main estimates under finance, vote No. 499, "Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, $35,000,000". Just above that may be found vote No. 498, "wartime prices and trade board, administration, $6,410,000". If the amounts that were to be spent by boards operating under these orders in council were to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund without its being necessary for parliament to provide the money the hon. member's point would be perfect. It would be blank cheque legislation; it would be on all fours with the legislation we attacked in 1931. That is not the situation. As a matter of fact, the form of this resolution is the form which this house has passed repeatedly under similar conditions. For instance, when we propose to authorize the formation of any new department like the Department of Veterans Affairs, which dispersed as much as $700 million in the course of a year, we do not put any figure in the resolution. The reason we do not put any figure in the resolution is that we have to vote the money separately. When we do vote the money we have most specific resolutions. A great number of them go through with the amounts of each vote provided in these resolutions.
I have, in my hand a copy of Hansard for the session of 1944, volume 2. On page 1638 may be found such resolutions as this:
That it is expedient to provide for a Department of Veterans Affairs to replace in part the Department of Pensions and National Health and to assume the management and control of and to consolidate in such department all matters not by law assigned to any other department relating to the care, treatment, training or reestablishment of members and former members of the armed forces and other persons and all such other matters as may from time to time be assigned; and to provide further for the appointment of such officers, clerks and employees as are necessary for the proper and efficient administration of the act.
Generally speaking, that is the form of resolution which is passed when you are vesting a department, a board, a commission, or any other body, with authority to disperse money and employ officers, servants and agents. That is the reason for the form of this resolution.

Emergency Powers
The hon. member takes exception to the fact that we have combined these various orders in council dealing with disparate matters in one bill. I must say that we never would enact new legislation in this way. If there were any danger whatever that this was a precedent for bringing along new legislation and combining various subject matters in one bill and putting it in one schedule I would be alarmed. We never would do that. The schedule to this bill is a schedule of orders in council, all of which are the law now and have been the law for years, some of them for more than nine years. They are well known to people who have been interested in them. They are not new. All this legislation does is to prevent these orders in council from lapsing, while it allows everything else to lapse. That is all it does. It just prevents these from lapsing. Under these circumstances I do not think it is proper to describe it as a combination of fifty-seven different bills.
It must be borne in mind that when the house passed the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act and extended it in 1946 it gave sanction not to fifty-seven orders in council but to six or seven thousand. The house passed that legislation without hon. members having any of these orders in council before them on their desks. The orders in council were accessible to them; they could be consulted, but they were not put in a schedule to a bill. It is entirely inconsistent to swallow six or eight thousand orders in council without looking at them, by passing legislation, and then to object to passing fifty-seven orders in council which are before hon. members. That is the situation here. I thought this matter was given a great deal of consideration as to what was the proper thing to do.
I said that this had been done in Great Britain and in Australia, and I was told that it did not make any difference what they did there; that we have our own democracy and should follow our own rules. I wholly agree. I would' not follow a certain course of procedure because it was followed in Great Britain, in Australia, or in the United States. But if the reasons for taking a certain course in Great Britain were sound, or for 'taking a certain course in the United States or Australia were sound, and the same reasons existed here, the fact that they took a certain course would raise the presumption that we were not very far wrong in taking the same course.
In Great Britain and in Australia they had the same problems before them. I have the bills before me. The name of the bill in Great Britain is the Emergency Laws Transitional Provisions Act of 1946. It has a long schedule
with all kinds of regulations. They call them regulations over there. Our own orders in council are regulations by orders in council. Here are many pages of regulations dealing with all kinds of things. All this act did was to pick up what was the law of the land then by regulation and say that these that are appended to the bill shall not lapse. It is quite a different matter from initiating new legislation. They did the same thing in Australia. Provision apparently was made for amendment to them by the house.
I thought I tried to make it clear at an earlier stage of this discussion that the government is not taking power to legislate by order in council. The government has been accused of wanting power to legislate by order in council instead of legislating in the house. I made it clear, I thought, earlier in the session that by this legislation we were saying, "No longer shall we have any power whatever to make any changes in these orders in council or to pass any orders in the fields covered by these orders in council. We shall have no power to do that any longer. We shall retain the power to revoke the orders in council in whole or in part, but these orders in council are frozen." Parliament expresses its will in the matter. It places its imprimatur upon these orders in council and says, "Under that code you must operate during the remainder of the time and under no other."
I do not know whether I need1 to go over again the principles upon which these orders in council were selected. They are orders in council which are expected to be required for a short period of indefinite duration. I cannot put it any more briefly than that. Some of these orders in council will be revoked within a matter of weeks; some of them will be revoked within a matter of months; some of them will run the whole year; and as to some of them, we may need to come back and ask that parliament extend them further at the end of the year, depending upon what developments are. Provision will be made in the act for the presentation of an address, so that parliament can do that. But parliament will do it; it will not be the governor in council. In no sense will it be legislation by order in council. There do not seem to be any good or practical reasons why we should take orders in council which may last for only a few weeks or only a few months and pass separate bills regarding them.
My hon. friend speaks about the confusion that the reader of the statutes will have when he sees in the same statute book an act relating to veterans preference and an order in council appended to this so-called omnibus bill. The position will be perfectly clear. 1
Emergency Powers

think, to the reader of the statutes. Undoubtedly, when that statute takes effect, the order in council will be revoked. Perhaps the statute itself will revoke the order in council. That would make it clear beyond peradventure that there are not two acts but only one, under which the veterans preference is provided. The reason why we did not introduce a bill at the beginning of the session was that we were given to understand; or perhaps I should not say that we were given to understand, but rather that we thought, from the representations which we had received and the controversy which there had been, that this matter of veterans preference would create a great deal of discussion, and that the proper way to deal with it was to refer it to a committee. I do not know now whether that is to be done or not, but we did not [DOT] think there was any reasonable prospect of that bill, if we introduced it, becoming law before March 31; and certainly it would not have, as events have proved, because so much time has been taken with other legislation such as the wheat board legislation. In that situation, where it ought to be incorporated in legislation, where you know you cannot get your legislation through before March 31, where there may be much controversy about it, and where a reasonable way of dealing with it, as we thought, was to refer it to a committee of the house, what was the sensible thing to do? Was not the sensible thing to do to continue this order in council until the legislation should be passed, at which time the order in council would be revoked?
The same or substantially the same considerations apply to the old age pensions legislation and also to the labour relations legislation. In those cases there were special reasons why we thought it was impracticable to have our legislation enacted before this emergency act lapsed, and therefore we decided that we should continue it and not let it lapse, but have our legislation introduced as soon as we could. If we break up this schedule now and introduce a number of bills, each with its first, second and third reading in this house and in the senate, it will immensely prolong our work during this session, and I do not see any reason for doing so. This case does not create a precedent for new legislation. This is a situation which arises once in a lifetime; perhaps it will never arise again. It is a situation which arises at the end of a great war, when you have many emergency orders in council, some of which must not be allowed to lapse; some of which will run for a short time and some for a longer time. In that case it appeared to us to be the practical and right course to

gather them up and, if they were orders in council which would be required for a short period of indefinite duration, put them in one bill and then get rid of them by revocation from time to time as the occasion might require.
There was another class of orders altogether that we replaced by legislation, such as the wheat board orders. There was a large number of orders that we replaced by legislation, but the careful selection was made of these for the reasons I have mentioned. It is a course of procedure which parallels that taken by other peoples in other countries who were confronted with a similar problem. It is a course of procedure which economizes the time of this house in a session which promises to be very long anyway. It is not blank cheque legislation. It does not create any dangerous precedent. It affords the house an opportunity of discussing every one of these measures seriatim in committee of the whole when the bill is before the committee. In my judgment, it is a course which should receive the support of the house.

I feel that I should
make my position clear with respect to my view as to the proper procedure in regard to this resolution while it is in committee. The hon. member for Quebec South referred to the fact that I had said the purpose of the committee was to consider whether or not it was expedient to continue controls. Probably my language was not sufficiently definite, and I thank the hon. member for bringing it to my attention. I should have said the committee must decide, according to this resolution, whether it is expedient to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war, and also with respect to the other words in the resolution.
The hon. member for Stanstead suggested that I should allow full discussion on this resolution. I wish to assure him and all other hon. members that this is my view also; but
I do suggest as strongly as possible that the discussion should be on the resolution, not on extraneous matters and not on the bill. When I was speaking the other day with regard to the point of order I referred to Sir Thomas Erskine May's Parliamentary Procedure, fourteenth edition, from which I read these words:
Debate in committee on a financial resolution is confined 'to the terms of the resolution itself and must not be extended to the related bill.
This house has adopted a form of procedure. Briefly it is as follows. On money matters there is first a resolution. To my mind, discussion on the resolution, should be along the line of whether or not it is advisable to bring in such a resolution, instead of going into the details of what the bill will be. After the resolution is adopted, a bill is introduced and given first reading. Second reading is not given immediately; an opportunity is afforded hon. members to consider the legislation; and the following day, or some later day, when they have had that opportunity, second reading is moved in the house. At that time a full discussion of the principle is permitted. Then the bill is referred to committee, where questions may be asked as to the details of the bill.
What I am endeavouring to do is to direct the attention of the committee to the resolution, not to the bill. I realize that it is very difficult. I believe all information should be given hon. members to enable them to decide intelligently whether or not this resolution should be adopted and whether it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders, and so on. All necessary information should be given to enable hon. members to come to a conclusion as to whether it is desirable to provide for the continuation of the orders; but when we discuss the bill itself we are far from the resolution. A number of hon. members have mentioned certain regulations and suggested that they should not be included in the bill. I repeat what I said1 previously. If one hon. member mentions one regulation, such as old age pensions, and says that should not be in the bill, there would be no reason why another hon. member should not bring up and discuss some other regulation and say it should not be in the bill, there would be no reason why each of these fifty-seven regulations could not be discussed at this time. I submit to the committee that is not the purpose of the consideration of this resolution. I believe any discussion as to whether or not certain regulations should be in the bill should be left over until the bill itself is before the committee. If at that time the committee does not think

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have listened this afternoon to the discussion of a question which I believe is of great importance, namely the cost to the country of price control. As a result of propaganda that has been continued throughout the period of the war, and since, there has been embedded in the minds of the people a terrible fear of what will happen to them and to the country in the event of price controls being discontinued.
As a matter of fact, there has been propaganda-I am sure it was not intentional-which has consisted of building up a comparison between United States and Canadian costs of commodities. The result is that people are fearful of any change taking place in the whole matter of prices. I believe there has never been any fair comparison made by setting the cost of living indices of the United States and Canada alongside each other. That does not tell the picture at all. In order to have a proper picture it would be necessary to have the taxation levels of these two countries. And from information all of us have available to us it would appear that, on incomes under $3,000, the income tax in the United States is materially less than it is in Canada. In addition to that, with the exception of a number of states, in the United States they do not pay a sales tax such as we have in Canada. These are elements which must be taken into consideration.
I have the full information Before me respecting our own cost of living index, as it is contained in a pamphlet entitled "Wartime Controls", issued by the wartime information board in Ottawa on September 12, 1944. This contains particulars as to how the index is made up. So far as that cost of living index is concerned today, based as it is in many instances upon commodities no longer in production-much less in consumption-the index gives a false picture in that it creates a delusion based upon the fact that non-existent goods do not rise in price. In other words, it is based on unrealities in that it is based on various commodities which are no longer being produced.
The hon. member for Stanstead raised a good point when he asked how much this subsidy system, has cost the country. I have seen various estimates. According to the estimates contained in the reports of the wartime prices and trade board and the stabilization board, the total would be approximately $650 million, which would include some $54 83166-115
million for administration. But those estimates do not tell the story at all, because they do not give the cost of some of the methods employed by the government, such as the suspension of customs duty, the remission of excise taxes and so on, all of which reduce the public revenue.
I should like to deal with a commodity which is in short supply, not only in Canada but in other parts of the world, a commodity which is controlled in Canada by international agreement. I intend to take sugar and the sugar control as an indication of how the picture revealed by the report of the wartime prices and trade board is not correct. On page 1505 of Hansard there appears an answer given to the hon. member for Lethbridge in connection with raw cane sugar. It is stated there that the government lost some $233,834 in a twelve months period on its operations in connection with sugar. However, a little later on it states that other revenues resulted in the sugar administration operating at a profit of $287,951. I ask the minister: What are the other revenues of the sugar administration? Has the sugar administration been permitted to run some other business? If so, what is the nature of the investment that it has made?
I go on from there to submit that, while the answer on March 19 states that there was an operating profit of $287,951 in connection with sugar, that statement does not reveal the story at all. Instead of there having been a profit, there was actually a loss of several million dollars. I am going to place certain figures before the minister in order that he may make an answer. If my computations be correct, instead of the sugar administration making an operating profit of $287,951 out of its sugar and other businesses, the loss in fact amounted to almost $7,000,000 in revenues to the people of Canada.
The figure given on page 1508 of Hansard show that the sugar administrator obtained thirty-five per cent of his 1947 supply of sugar from Cuba, Santa Domingo and other countries in connection with which there is normally a duty of $1.29 per hundredweight.

It is estimated that 213,000 tons of sugar will be imported from the countries I have named, and normally the customs duties on that sugar would amount to $5,517,000. In other words, while the sugar administration claims that it made $287,951, it fails to show that in making that it lost $5,517,000 in customs duties.

I pass on from there to the other countries. Forty-seven per cent, or 287,000 tons, will come from other British countries, and the preference duty in these cases is twenty-nine cents per hundredweight. This represents a further loss to the country of approximately $1,665,000. In other words, as a result of sugar control there is a total of $7,182,000 lost to the revenues of this country during the current year. Subtracting what is given as the profit leaves a loss of $6,894,000, by reason of the remission or whatever you call it when customs duties are not charged. I might mention that Canada is the only country of the three countries in the sugar pool which is not collecting normal duties.
We come now to the local situation. Our domestic beet sugar production will be 222,000,000 pounds this year. If the domestic production of sugar were encouraged sufficiently to engage the full capacity of our factories there would be produced 320,000,000 pounds. We are in an international pool, but if the production of beet sugar were encouraged Canada's share would be immeasurably increased. If the other of the two large factories in Ontario were in production there would be an additional 50,000,000 pounds of sugar produced in Canada, which would make a greater supply of sugar available to Canada as well as encouraging an industry in this country.
The figures given in connection with the sugar control picture do not establish the true loss to this country. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said today that we want the whole picture, and that is what we are asking for.

That is the purpose of the discussion at this time. We want to find out what the picture actually is. On the one hand, we have a statement showing the benefits of control, but that statement fails to place before the people the picture with reference to what it is costing the taxpayers to apply this control. I should like the minister to take up not only sugar but the various other commodities with respect to which duties have been remitted or withdrawn or postponed. We would then have the picture before us as to the real cost. The estimate of $650 million given in the reports of the wartime prices and trade board and the stabilization board covers merely one side of the question. It does not cover the tens, yes, hundreds of millions of dollars represented by tariffs, by excise not charged and by other matters to which reference can be made later. I ask the minister to give the committee, as I

know he will, a full statement, so that for once we shall know in this country the actual position.
We hear so much about how much lower prices are in Canada than in the United States. But as a matter of fact within the past month, in the United States prices of commodities from which the ceiling has been lifted, after having risen in December and January last, and particularly in December, to a high level, receded gradually until today in most cases prices on comparative commodities are not any higher in Canada than in the United States; and if consideration were given to the difference in wage levels between the two countries and in taxes and other elements that go into the cost of living and to availability, to which I made reference earlier, the argument that we have heard so often used in the past that price control is placing us in Canada in an immeasurably better position than the people of the United States would be found not to be so applicable today. As a matter of fact, the "Letter Review of Toronto", in a very full review made in the latter part of January of prices of all commodities, clothing, food and all the things ordinarily used by the average household, as between the city of Toronto and the city of Buffalo, shows that, while there was an increase in prices in the United States when price control was removed, the increased production resulted in availability, and availability resulted' in a return to more or less normalcy in the matter of prices. At the moment I am not advocating one thing more than another. I am just placing before the committee these comparative figures.
Further, Mr. Chairman, the Bank of Canada has put out various charts and graphs showing relative wage rates and commodity prices in the United States and Canada, but all these graphs that I have seen have been in respect of prices in the months of November and December, 1946. I have seen none for February or March, 1947. I would ask the minister to place before the committee on Monday, if it is possible for him to do so, a comparison showing wage rates and cost of living index as between the two countries as of today, for the graphs hitherto have been comparisons for November and December, 1946, when it is admitted that prices in the United States were high.

I gather, Mr. Chairman, that after what was said by the last speaker, the debate is now wide open, and that I can say the one or two things I wish to say.
The hon. member for Lake Centre stated that considerable propaganda was being spread in favour of price control. He said that he did not think the propaganda was being spread consciously but that the impression left by certain reports, and comparisons made in government statistics, was that price control was saving money for the people of Canada. I do not know whether propaganda has been spread either consciously or unconsciously in favour of price control, but I know definitely that there has been a great deal of propaganda against price control.
The cost of price control to the people of Canada was mentioned as being something over $600 million. But the people of Canada can only mean all the people of Canada, and if price control cost the people of Canada $600 million or whatever the actual figure was, that cost was reflected in lower prices to all the people of this country. It is just as broad as it is long. Whatever the cost may have been in taxes it 'was represented in the saving to the people wrhen they purchased goods. In my opinion, there is not the slightest doubt in the world that, since price control came into effect in this country not only has it saved the people of Canada money in the cost of. the things they had to buy, but because they were able to buy and because we had orderly rationing and stabilized prices we not only saved dollars and cents, but also saved in the health and strength of our people and in the orderliness of our society. These are gains that cannot be measured in dollars and cents, and there is no doubt that these gains have been made.
I imagine that the hon. member for Lake Centre is receiving letters from organizations and individuals in his constituency as I am from individuals and organizations in mine, protesting against any quick removal of price control. These letters come from responsible organizations. I am sorry I have not my file with me or I would mention their names. But propaganda is not necessary to convince the housewife of the value of price control when she goes to market and finds that, without price control, she has to pay ten, twenty or thirty per cent more than she had to pay last week for the same article when price control was in effect.

speechtext: Why not make it eighty per cent?

You can get it for a while. You can get it if there is a scarcity of goods, and when you come to the time when supply more than equals the demand artificial scarcities will be created, as they have been created in the past, in order to maintain prices.

I do not know whether it is necessary or not. It would not be necessary in a properly organized society, but it is done in the cut-throat society we have today. That is what I am saying. We should be clear about what we decide here.
If price controls are removed those of us in this house will not feel it much. A family getting $6,000 a year is in the middle or high income brackets. But take the thousands and hundreds of thousands of families in Canada who are receiving $1,500 or $1,000 a year. The removal of price controls is an important factor in the lives of these people where every cent has to be counted. I know these people. They are people who have to consider whether they will take a street car or walk and save six cents. These are considerations in the lives of the common people of this country. When I hear people talking for big business which is interested in exploiting the people of Canada, and not their social welfare, I feel that there is something radically wrong with our outlook on life.
I suppose controls will go within a brief period of time, but when they do, there will be organizations and delegations, many of them, on the doorstep of the government-and I do not care who that government will be- insisting that controls be imposed in order that they may make a living. Controls will be imposed.
I read in the Ottawa Journal yesterday that report of a debate in the Ontario legislature. In that debate Mr. Acres, a Progressive Conservative member, suggested a pretty complete control over the distribution of milk. He suggested that cities and towns in the province should be divided into zones and that certain deliveries be made only in those zones. According to the same report, the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario said that although there was a scarcity of dairy products, dairy farmers of Ontario had difficulty in selling their milk. Surely there is something wrong in a society of that kind.

The Ottawa Evening Journal. The dispatch reads as follows:
Washington, March 26-(BUP)-President Truman today expressed concern over high prices and advised business to make reductions where-ever possible.
Mr. Truman told a news conference he hoped prices would not continue to rise, lest a serious inflationary spiral set in.
The President added that he hoped business would see the handwriting on the wall so this spiral would not take place.
He pointed out that some major industries already have cut the prices on their products. He expressed the hope that other businesses would follow suit.
Mr. Truman was asked to elaborate on his phrase-handwriting on the wall.
This meant, he said, that he did not want to see a spiral in prices which would cause inflation and lead to another round of new wage demands. This process could be endless if prices continue to rise, the President said.
My information is that the hope of lower prices in the United States has been largely disappointed. I shall get the figures so that I shall not be talking generally; I hope that the hon. member for Lake Centre was not.

That may be the point of view of the minister, and undoubtedly it is if he says it is. This dominion will be eighty years of age if it holds together until July 1 next, and for fully three-quarters of that time the chief sources of revenue, the chief sources of money to pay the expenses of running the country were two: they were the import duties and the excise taxes. There was a blessed day when there were no income taxes, believe it or not, and when we relied almost entirely upon duties collected at the customs ports and upon taxes collected by excise officers. It is submitted that any remission of these duties and taxes means that they must be made up in other ways or by other taxes, and that where they have been remitted as a part of the system of control they constitute part of the cost of control. If the dollar a hundredweight, which was collected in excise on the refining of sugar, is not there to pay for some expenditure of the dominion, the Minister of Finance must find that dollar somewhere else. It merely means that the control has cost us that dollar, and in my point of view it is part of the cost of control just as much as a direct subsidy.

speechtext: The housing plans of the government are remarkably free from government subsidy as compared with the housing plans of other countries, as members of this house know. For years the most extraordinary pressure has been brought to bear on the government to go into a system of state subsidies to housing. It is fair to say that these housing schemes are not wholly devoid of possible subsidy, nor have they ever been. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What I have to ask the
minister has a direct bearing on the matter before the committee. This afternoon, in reply to the hon. member for Lake Centre, or Stanstead, I have forgotten which, the minister quoted from the Ottawa Journal, indicating that, at times, he does place some credence in newspaper reports.
On the front page of tonight's Journal there is a brief item, two paragraphs of which are as follows:
A timetable for full decontrol of the Canadian economy is expected to be announced shortly by the prices 'board.
The coming decontrol order will contain future dates for the lifting of price ceilings from the greatest part of consumer commodities still subject to restriction.
If the report is correct, are we to understand that the government, or the wartime prices and trade board, proposes to announce to vendors of consumer goods the date ahead when prices will be lifted, and allow them to

1S03
Emergency Powers
hoard between now and then those goods which are in short supply, and then take advantage of increased prices?
I gave an example of what is taking place at the present time when I referred to Kleenex, ini speaking the other day in another debate. If one wants some things, he finds it almost impossible to get them, while other things that one does not require he can get in abundance.
One can go to Woolworth's or Kresge's, or any of those stores, and buy the flat connections for flatirons or toasters, by the bushel. No one wants them. Everyone has them. However they probably have a large quantity on hand, and want to sell them. But if one wants an ordinary little plug to plug into a wall socket for a lamp, he cannot buy it. Both of these articles are made of exactly the same material, and both must be made all the time. The ones one cannot get now must have been made during the war for the various military offices and for industrial establishments. They must be in existence. Why are they being held up?
If these things are in short supply, or anything from which they are made-I believe there is some metal in them-as is indicated in the newspaper article, does the government propose to tell manufacturers and sellers when they can expect a rise in price, and then take the public for another little ride, such as we have had in the last two years?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am sure the minister must know whether the wartime prices and trade board proposes to commit this action, or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then I should like to express the hope that the government will not permit action of that kind in connection with goods in short supply.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not wish to ask the minister anything concerning the opinion he read to the house the other day, and his comments on the Canada Temperance Act case. I understand he has told the house that in so far as this legislation is concerned, it rests on what it has pleased the government to describe as an emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And I am not going beyond that for the present. I am now anxious to know just what constitutes the emergency. I believe our purchases from the United States exceed substantially in dollars the amount of our sales to that country, and that settlement is becoming more and more difficult for us because we have not the dollars necessary to make settlement. Through many years we used to sell goods to the United States; but never-and I am not speaking of the war years-in normal years did we sell goods in value anywhere equalling the value of goods we bought from that country. We made settlement with the proceeds of the sale of our commodities to other countries, principally to Britain. At the present time our sales to Britain are not yielding us a return which enables us to meet our obligations in the United States. I am quite aware that the Minister of Justice has escaped from the burdens of the high office which he held for many years, but I know he is familiar with the financial and fiscal situation of the country. I should like him to tell the committee if this shortage of dollars to meet our United States obligations constitutes any part of the emergency with which the government says we are confronted at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Whether the shortage of dollars constitutes any part of the emergency relied upon?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should not like to say anything more about the emergency than what I said in my speech. I set out the nature of the emergency there and I think that is as complete as I can make it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not wish to contradict the minister; I did not understand that he attempted to enunciate in his speech all the causes of emergency upon which he was relying. He referred to the disparity between the rise in the cost of living in the United States and in Canada since the war. I do not wish to press that point unduly, but I think any fair person is bound to admit that that example is totally without value. We were told that the rise in the cost of living in the United States had been eighteen per cent and in Canada but six per cent. Nothing was put before the committee to show what were the taxes paid by a man in the United States, earning $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000 a year with one, two, three or more children, nor was that set opposite the taxes paid by a man in Canada who was similarly situated. The minister told us quite candidly that he had not taken into consideration any subsidies, bonuses or tax and duty remissions, so I submit that in so far as that example went it was totally without value.
The minister went on to talk about housing and the disorders he anticipated were the restrictions on tenancy removed. He did not dwell extensively upon the person who might find himself accommodated by the lifting of these controls. Nobody wishes to dispossess anyone in order to leave a house vacant; decontrol would have the effect of putting someone else into the house and frequently it would be the owner who by some accident, absence at war or some other cause of that kind, is denied access to his own home and prevented from the enjoyment of that which is his own.
The minister gave some other instances in connection with prices. 1 do not think we can rely upon that information until we know to what extent the taxpayer in Canada pays for what he buys over and above the purchase price in the form of taxes which are given to the vender to make up for what he loses through the control. A number of the instances which the minister gave vanished before the inquiry which has gone on while this resolution has been under consideration.
I do not think the1 minister was attempting to give a full list of all the causes of the emergency. Many people who are familiar with national affairs and who are deeply interested in the prosperity of the country feel that the unbalance in our trade which has

resulted in a shortage of dollars to pay the obligations becoming due in the United States is a cause for grave alarm. Some consider that it is one of the most alarming questions which confront the government and the nation today. I should like the minister to say if, in his opinion, the fact that there is a shortage of dollars to pay debts that are accruing in the United States is a matter of grave concern to the government and if, in consequence, it constitutes a part of what it has pleased the government to call the emergency which is being dealt with in this legislation.
Mr. ILSLEY; It did not occur to me that that was part of the emergency which is the basis for this legislation. This afternoon the hon. member for Broadview pointed out the dangers of a Minister of Justice outlining too fully the exact legal grounds upon which the government relies. For instance, if we were taken into the courts on this we would define, I presume with considerable clearness, exactly the nature of the emergency being relied upon, but I do not think the House of Commons is the place to do that. I consider that the speech I made on March 20 was sufficient to indicate the emergency which would serve as a basis for this legislation and the economic controls. My considerations are set out on pages 1584 and 1585 of Hansard.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There are five of these orders in council which deal with people of the Japanese race, and I would ask the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Labour for some explanation about these orders. One of them is listed as under the Department of Fisheries; there are two under the Department of Labour and two under the Department of the Secretary of State. The one under the Department of Fisheries is an order in council prohibiting persons of Japanese racial origin from fishing on the Pacific coast. I should like to know whether this order is included in this bill because that restriction is to continue only until this bill expires, or whether the government has not yet decided what its permanent policy will be with regard to allowing Japanese to fish on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would my hon. friend make his question more specific? What does he want to know?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I want to know with regard to this order in council, in fact with regard to all five of them, whether they are included in this bill because they are to continue in existence only for a period of one year, or whether it is because the government has not yet decided what its permanent policy is to be with regard to the matters covered by these orders.
First of all, as regards the order in council preventing Japanese from fishing on the Pacific coast, I would point out to the committee that for many years it has been the policy of' the Canadian government that all the fishing on that coast shall be done by white British subjects and Canadian Indians. I have in my hand the annual report of the Department of Fisheries for the year 1925-26- that is twenty-two years ago-and at page 53 I find this statement under the heading "Reduction in Orientals";
The department's policy of eliminating the oriental from the fisheries of the province-
That is the province of British Columbia. *-with a view to placing the entire industry in the hands of white British subjects and Canadian Indians appears to be working out well as is shown by statement No. 10.
Further on, under the same heading I find this statement:
It is the intention to continue this percentage-
Referring to the percentage of reduction of oriental licences each year.
-each year until these industries are entirely in the hands of whites or Canadian Indians.
Those are the fishing industries on the Pacific coast. They have been in the hands of whites and Canadian Indians since the evacuation of the Japanese from the Pacific coast during the war. I want to know with regard to this order in council whether the government intends to continue that policy which has been in force for many years, or whether the policy is to be allowed to lapse with the lapsing of this omnibus bill, and then the Japanese will again be permitted to fish on the Pacific coast.
I have much the same question to ask with regard to the second order in council, which is under the Department of Labour, P.C. 946, and deals with the evacuation and relocation of persons of the Japanese race in Canada; and a similar question with regard to the next order in council, P.C. 7355, which deals with financial assistance to voluntary repatriates to Japan and for liquidation and transfer of their assets to Japan.
Then I should like to hear from the Secretary of State with regard to the other two orders relating to the Japanese. One is P.C. 1665, and is described as "Administration by the custodian of property of persons of the Japanese race"; the other is P.C. 469, "Transfer to the custodian of the property of Japanese evacuees". It seems to me that the two last orders in council are in a different category from the first three. The last two deal with the property of the Japanese in the hands of the custodian.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can answer in a few simple words. The policy with respect to the relocation of the Japanese is to be continued during the life of the bill which the hon. member referred to as the omnibus bill. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Did the minister say that no Japanese or that some Japanese will be permitted to return there?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I think the policy that we have been pursuing in the relocation of the Japanese across the dominion is in their own best interests. With respect to the return to Japan of anyone who desires to go there, that policy will be continued. Already about 4,000 have returned to Japan. I think that answers my hon. friend.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. The question I asked was whether the policy as represented by these orders in council was to continue in effect only for the life of the omnibus bill, which will be for a period of one year with the possibility of an extension for a further year; is it the final policy of the government that this restriction will apply only for the life of the bill?

May I say at once that that certainly would be a matter for further consideration.
In reference to the question raised by the hon. member with regard to fisheries and not referred to by the Minister of Labour, may I say I can speak with exactitude in regard to the nature of the order in council. Steps have been taken to prohibit absolutely and completely fisheries along the Pacific coast, at least for a certain period. My hon. friend's problem and mine is not during the period of this legislation; it is the establishment of a certain amount of security for our people over a period of five or ten years, and the protections that this house has seen fit to take and keep for the security of our own people along the security zone of British Columbia. I think that is the worry of my hon. friend. He may feel that this may lapse possibly with the effluxion of time. When these things lapse-I am speaking only for myself as an individual-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

Perhaps even then I can speak with greater authority than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, because I think the chances are if I want to be here that I have a far better opportunity of being on this side of the house than the hon. member who has interrupted me so unneces-

sarily. May I say that, even though the hon. member for Vancouver South and I disagree on many problems, we disagree with my hon. friend on this problem. This is the problem of British Columbia, and we are as one in our viewpoint with regard to future legislation. There are two great issues

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is nothing wrong with that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The pioneer behind me says that there is nothing wrong with that, because when no other voice was heard in the Commons with regard to what we look upon as a vital problem in British Columbia, the voice of the hon. member for New Westminster, now joined by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, the hon. member for Vancouver North, the hon. member for Kamloops, the hon. member for Nanaimo and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, was heard. We are all as one; we are no longer a lone band of fighting forces for the cause of British Columbia. In regard to this issue in this house we are a united body. We have to face certain difficulties-and my hon. friend knows that-in regard to our obligations and to the united nations charter, especially under sections 55 and 56. I believe these things can all be worked out satisfactorily. But there is one thing; if I know my province which I have represented now for nearly thirty years, and which my hon. friend has represented for a long time; if I know my province, which had only one lone voice in these halls for many years in regard to this oriental problem, the members from British Columbia, regardless of their political affiliations will stand as one in regard to the maintenance of these principles they have had in regard to the security of our people. It is a question of security in British Columbia. On the establishment of that security we stand together. We want to tell our good friends from the other provinces that we shall stand together upon this issue, come what may.

So far as I am concerned, this is my closing observation and I address it to the Minister of Justice in terms of an appeal for a reasonable procedure which will save the time of the house in the long run. I for one had looked forward to the sittings of this committee in the hope of deriving from the ministers a great deal of information which would be of considerable assistance to myself and, I believe, to other hon. members on the later stages of the bill. In view of the ruling that was made, information of a detailed nature has not been forthcoming and discussion has been confined to more general questions.
We have had it made clear during the course of this discussion, quite apart from the opening statement of the Minister of Justice, that the orders were of three kinds: regulative, administrative and legislative. A further break-down is possible. We have had a statement from the minister that there are certain of these orders which are themselves to be the subject matter of bills to be introduced at this session: the old age pensions orders, P.C. 1003 dealing with labour relations, and those dealing with veterans preference in the civil service. I am urging on the Minister of Justice that the course which ought to be taken even at this hour is a course which will lead the government to bring in separate measures. I urge him now, once this resolution is reported, to bring in the bills which they have indicated they intend to bring down at this session on these particular matters, so that at least these matters may be dealt with apart from the omnibus bill and be considered on their own merits.
The difficulty we have been up against- and it was, I think, quite apparent from the time the ruling was made in the committee confining discussion-is that there is bound to be a great deal of confusion and it is confusion which will take up the time of the house. That confusion will not be lessened by simply being told by the government, "Oh, well, you will have an opportunity of getting the information in detail in committee after second reading." It is all very well to assume that the house is just going to slur over the matter of second read-

ing in order to get into committee again. I ask the minister in all fairness and reasonableness to ask himself how members of the opposition, who are here to do their duty as members of this house, are to be able to discern the principle of a bill of this kind, which proposes to extend the life of fifty-seven orders in council-because they have not yet been reduced in number-of three distinct kinds, and containing some orders which are to be the subject matter of bills to be introduced later this session. As the hon. member for Quebec South put it, some of the fifty-seven orders are good and some of them are not good. How can a hodge-podge like that fail to create confusion in the house and prolong debate? I urge on the Minister of Justice even at this late hour that the course of expediency is not that indicated in the resolution, namely, that one bill be introduced for this general purpose, but rather that the government ought to break this measure down into a number of bills so that there can be an orderly approach to them, both on second reading and in committee of the whole, on the part of members of the house.

I have a problem which I should like to put before the minister so that he may give it consideration before the bill is introduced. I have had a good many complaints about the eviction order under the wartime prices and trade board, not with regard to housing but with regard to commercial properties. These complaints have been particularly from men who have served five and six years overseas. In some instances these men were in business before they enlisted in the armed service. They closed up their places of business. They spent five or six years fighting for this country. They came home, and when they endeavoured to get a place in which to do business and rehabilitate themselves, they were unable to do so. In several instances, these men bought properties, but up to date they have been unable to get possession of them.
I should like to cite one particular case, that of a young man who was in business up until 1940. In that year he closed his business and enlisted in the navy, serving five years, four and a half of which were on the high seas. He came back home in the fall of 1945 and endeavoured, as I say, to rehabilitate himself. He was not able to get a suitable place. He purchased a store on the main street of the town. That store had been rented from month to month by a man who had an opportunity during the war to cash in on a first-class business. This young man, in order to get started, finally was able to lease the back part of a small warehouse at one end of the town, for which accommodation he had to pay twice the rent he is getting for his own store, which is situated in one of the best business sections of the town.
I am bringing this forward at this time, for the simple reason that I hope the minister will give it consideration and will see to it that one particular order is eliminated from the bill-which in my opinion would not cause any hardship on any person-and that at least veterans who have served this country for a
number of years may be able to secure possession of their own commercial properties and get themselves back into business again. I trust that the minister will give this matter his earnest consideration, and that he will take it up with the Minister of Finance who, I am sure, will consider it with him.
