speechtext:
I think there is one field which
has not been covered by the Minister of Justice in any statement he has made so far and which ought to be covered by some member of the government, since it has an important bearing on this whole question. I am very glad to see the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply in the chamber because this is a subject with which he is particularly fitted to deal.
I wish to talk for a moment about the subject of production. We have had a great deal of talk about controls, their effect in maintaining present prices and in preventing inflation. and all the other very worthy objects, and of course we are all in favour of preventing inflation. But the question of production has been giving many of us on this side of the house a great deal of concern, and before we come to consider this legislation it might be fitting for the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to make a comprehensive statement as to the difficulties he must have found in getting production of building materials under way in view of the policies of the wartime prices and trade board. For instance, I have the statement of the Prime Minister on January 31, 1946, with which I wholly agree, when he said:
The one satisfactory answer to the danger of inflation is more and more production.
Many of us in the house would be much more content to grant continuation of the controls for which the government is asking if we could believe that such continuation, at least under present policies, would lead to increased production and, what is more important, if we could believe that it would not lead to a decrease in production. I have here the report of the wartime prices and trade board up to February 1, 1947. I wish to refer to a few statements made in this report, because they bear closely on the question of how controls affect production.
First, I want to point out to the committee, as I have pointed out before on the question of housing, that last year the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who had just started and, I think, most energetically, to stimulate building production, stated in this house what he had to do in order to get
Emergency Powers

increased production of various lines of goods. In every case he had to go against the price control policy of the government. He will remember that he had to get more bricks, and that necessitated a price increase of bricks. He will remember that, in order to bring about an increase in the capacity of plants producing plumbing fixtures and materials, he had to give those plants an incentive subsidy. He will remember that in some cases he had to guarantee a market for excess production in order to induce some manufacturers to increase their productive capacity at prevailing price levels. I could go on and on. Of course he has given double depreciation and tax relief, all in order to carry out the same good purpose. That is what concerns me tonight, and I wish to refer to some of the statements in this report of the wartime prices and trade board which bear out what I say. First, I want to refer to page 39, where the production of lumber is being dealt with. I find this paragraph:
In the course of 1946, there were a number of price adjustments applying to lumber and lumber products. They were necessitated by increased costs of production, inadequate output of certain lines, and by difficulties in distribution and grading.
There we have a direct statement of inadequate production. Again reference is made to the increase of twenty per cent made in October, 1946, in the price of red cedar shingles. I remember, as I know the minister will remember, the circumstances under which that increase was granted, after a regular outburst by the people producing those shingles which simply could not be denied. Again on page 40 I find this:
In November, 1946, ceiling prices of doors, screen doors and windows, and door and window frames were increased twenty per cent and a twenty-five per cent increase was authorized in the price of sash ... In the previous April the timber control had made arrangements for the production of a substantial quantity of these doors which had been off the market for some time because of the low basic period prices established for them.
At this juncture I wish to point out that in every case the price advance which brought these goods back into production followed the building up of such a pressure that the wartime prices and trade board could no longer withstand it. That must inevitably be so, and I am not criticizing the officials of the wartime prices and trade board for it. I wonder for how long before the minister got on the job this holding down of production of the things which he stimulated had been going on, and how much production had been lost. If we are to continue these controls is there a policy which will see to it that any ill effect of the 
controls in regard to production is met before it becomes so acute and so obvious that action must be taken? If I turn to the paragraph on other construction products, on pages 40 and 41, I find exactly the same sort of statement made by the person who prepared the report. For instance, I see this paragraph:
The maximum prices of builders' hardware were also raised during the year. Some companies had discontinued the production of loss lines, while those manufacturers who had maintained production were in a position to demonstrate financial need.
Then comes this significant paragraph:
Towards the end of 1946 an additional criterion was admitted in pricing supplies which were urgently needed for the housing programme. When the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply advises that a particular building product is in critically short supply, the board is prepared to consider authorizing an increase in prices to induce additional production, even though the increases may not be warranted on the basis of over-all financial need.
In reading those words, it will be seen that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who, as we all know, is an energetic man, in order to carry out the task laid upon his shoulders of stimulating the production of building material had to get in there and get production going. When he found himself blocked by the then rigid policy of the board he had to bring about a change in that policy, and it is a change that hon. members on this side of the house in this party, suggested long before the minister actually brought it into effect. It would give me much more assurance that these controls eventually would come off, and much more assurance that, while they are on, they would be doing us some good, if I could feel that the policy which was introduced by the minister of reconstruction could be carried on generally, and not only in respect of building materials.
It seems to me that there must come a time in the decontrol programme when production becomes more important than holding prices at an artificial and unrealistic level. The choice of that time may be, as the minister has said, a matter of judgment; but there is a point before complete decontrol which is certainly a matter of judgment and when production must be considered. Perhaps I might give one other example as to what can happen, one which will be within the memory of all hon. members. They will recall a time, I believe it was at the beginning of April last year, when, for about four or five days, one could not buy a pound of butter in Ottawa. Then the four-cent increase was granted, and along came the butter. That is the tendency I am warning about.

Emergency Powers
As I have said, I would feel more sure of decontrol, and the policy of the government in connection therewith, if I could feel that the policy being followed was one of making the board the conscious instrument of the production of useful goods which, as the Prime Minister has said, is the only real cure for inflationary tendencies. I might go farther and say that if I could feel that the controls were being administered so as to be the conscious instrument of their own quick destruction, then again I think we would be better off.
I want to pass on for a moment to another matter vitally connected with this whole question of production and the maintenance of controls. It is this, that you have a much better case for the maintenance of the control of prices if, in fact, you control prices. But if you are not going to maintain the price level, and if prices rise, despite the maintenance of those controls, then it is questionable whether the maintenance of the controls is in the interests of the country, or that they are serving the purpose for which they were designed, which, as I understand at the present time, is the negative principle of maintaining price levels and not the positive principle of inducing production.
Let me give- an example of what I mean. The hon. member for Swift Current has already mentioned it. This evening he read from a newspaper report a rumour to the effect that prices were going to rise very shortly. I read the same thing some time ago in a Canadian Press dispatch, and it suggested that because subsidies on many articles would be coming off on March 31, and for other reasons, there would be a considerable increase in prices in the period April-May. It even went so far as to suggest that it was planned to decontrol about half the food items which are now controlled. The report to which I have referred was as specific as that.
If that is to be so, then the case the government makes for these controls becomes less and less useful. Let us not fool ourselves. If we are to maintain the machinery, and not maintain the prices, then hon. members to my left are not getting very much out of the simple maintenance of the machinery, and neither will the people of Canada.
I have referred to a report to which the hon. member for Swift Current directed the attention of the committee. I have another one, which I believe appeared in yesterday's Ottawa Journal. Apparently a delegation of property owners went to see the Minister of Finance. This is a report of what was said by Mr. W. J. LeClair, president of the Property Owners' Association. They presented their
brief on rent control to the Minister of Finance, and Mr. LeClair had this to say to the press:
Mr. Abbott made no comment, but he said he was faced with a decision on the problem very shortly, and that the brief came at an opportune time.
He said he was faced with the decision on the problem of whether or not to increase rents very shortly. Yet in the house the other day, when the hon. member for Eglinton asked the Minister of Finance that very question, and other questions of a similar nature, the minister gave no indication that very shortly he would have to make a decision as to whether or not rents would be increased.
There is one other important point. What was the significance of the resignation of Mr. Donald Gordon and of other senior officials, the picture of one of whom I saw in the paper only the other day-one who had resigned after having given good service during the war emergency? Can one believe Mr. Donald Gordon would have resigned his post had he not felt his job was over? Surely his job was that of protecting against inflation. Must he not feel that his job is virtually over?
When I was in Vancouver just before coming to Ottawa I talked to a house builder who told me it was impossible for him to enter into any contract for construction at a fixed price, because he did not know what was going to happen. This particular builder who was talking to me thought there would be decontrol on March 31, and that after that date he would be able to figure out his future business in the way he had prior to the war.
My suggestion to the government is this, that there will be a time when it will be better to make a clean break than to go on and try to ease it off, meanwhile not succeeding in your intention of releasing controls gradually.
I should like to refer to another matter which has amused me very much, and which again, has to do with the question of production, and whether or not the government can justify the keeping on of controls if it is not going to make them serve the purpose for which they were intended. My hon. friends to my left have taken up a week of the time of the house, when we could have been discussing more important matters-and I do not suppose they will like my saying this to them -in trying to put over what the Minister of Justice has referred to as their social policy. The very reason we in this party say that controls endanger freedom is that, no matter what the Minister of Justice may be trying to do, we know that the members of the party to our left want to maintain these controls as
Emergency Powers

an instrument of social policy, and not as an instrument of getting this country going, and of expanding its production-which, after all, is the only means of producing wealth. They want to do it to further their socialist aims.

Hon. members to my left are not really an opposition at all because they are just trying to further their own doctrine. I want to protect them from playing into the hands of big business. I want to bring to my support some important men whose names are household words among my hon. friends to my left. I am referring to the two officials of the government whom I think they love the best, Mr. Donald Gordon and Mr. McGregor, commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act. I do not think they are helping Mr. McGregor or Mr. Gordon in their work by the way they attempt to use them to further their own socialistic aims. I should like to tell the committee what Mr. Gordon said in 1945, I believe in January, with regard to the removal of price control. This is quoted with approval by Mr. McGregor in the report of the Department of Labour for the year ending March 31, 1945. Mr. Gordon said about price controls:
In some cases the continuance of such controls beyond the emergency would have the effect of restricting competition and production, and of strengthening the position of established businesses. I think you will agree that this would be most undesirable. To create a healthy and prosperous economy more competition and more freedom for newcomers to start up in business is needed-not less.
Then follows a sentence which I commend particularly to the Minister of Justice:
That is one of the principal reasons why such controls have to be eliminated as soon as feasible and before the emergency is quite gone rather than after.
That was an important statement by Mr. Gordon. He gave it as his opinion that the controls should be removed before the emer-

gency is quite gone, rather than after. Strangely enough he has said this to protect the people of this country from the monopolistic position which big corporations might be able to obtain during the period should decontrol be held off too long. I often think that if hon. members to my left paid more attention to facts, particularly to facts' of production, rather than trying to change the social system and not caring what happens to the country while they are doing it, we would all be much better off.
I referred to that passage not only for the benefit of hon. members to my left, but I commend it to the government as something they should keep in mind when they are considering decontrol. What is the emergency that we are facing? How is the government to decide when we have reached a point just before the end of the emergency when they should decontrol? Above all, do not let us go on maintaining controls as a heavy weight on production while at the same time we do not succeed in keeping prices from rising continually and perhaps to not very much less heights than they would rise if there were no controls at all?

The final paragraph on page 41 of the report of the wartime prices and trade board is very important. It reads:
While price increases may follow in the case of some of the other products released from control, they will frequently not exceed the advances which would have1 been necessary if price control had been continued. At the same time, producers will be free to correct anomalies in their price structures which may possibly result in some improvement in the pattern of production.
That is a significant statement and it is one which should be considered carefully by members of the government. Perhaps I have got a long way from what I was saying at the beginning of my remarks. I think it would be most helpful to members of the committee, including the hon. member who does not want my opinion, to hear that of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply on the effect of controls on construction material. I have just received from his department a pamphlet dealing with building materials and, even though he has stimulated construction considerably, in some cases he estimates that for 1947 the production of cement will be below the production in 1929. It is estimated that the production of building brick will be no less than 330,000,000 bricks below the 1929 production. It is estimated that the production of structural tile will be about 80,000 tons less than the 1929 production. It is estimated that the production of steel pipe, tubing and fittings likewise will be below the 1929 levels. It might be that if the minister's policy of giving price
increases as an incentive to production were followed generally he would be able to do much better than these figures. If that policy were followed throughout the whole range of articles under control we might all benefit from the increased production, which the Prime Minister says is the only real remedy for inflation. I wonder if we might hear from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The primary question that was asked of me was whether controls had hampered production. I can conscientiously say that since I have been associated with controls, which is from their inception, controls have never been permitted to hamper production. In fact, controls at the moment are greatly stimulating production in several important lines. In my opinion the over-all production today would not be improved by the immediate removal of controls. If the control of lumber were removed today-and lumber shows the greatest discrepancy between export and domestic prices of any commodity-I doubt if one additional tree would be cut. If the control of steel were removed, the over-all production of steel today would drop by at least twenty per cent. The reason is that under control we are able to take the surplus primary production from Sault Ste. Marie and move it to the finishing mills at Hamilton, Toronto and Montreal. We are able to bring billets from Sydney, Nova Scotia, something that is never done under ordinary conditions, and move them to Montreal and Hamilton and convert them into finished steel. Were this not possible, the over-all production of steel in this country would be at least twenty per cent less than it is at this moment.
There are certain commodities such as brick which are influenced by price. There are brickyards which are closed down and some which have been closed for years. One price will cause certain brickyards to open, and a higher price will perhaps bring into production one or two more yards. Then it becomes a question of what the public should pay for that increased production. It may be expensive. If the ordinary production at one price is three-million, is it worth a substantial price rise to bring the production to three-million-one? That is a matter of judgment.
Then we have the effect of price on diverting production from one line to another but not affecting the over-all production. Price differentials will cause a manufacturer to go into one line of production which returns a higher profit as against another line which he is equally well able to make but which shows a lower profit. Maladjustments of that kind
Emergency Powers

are, of course, corrected by price adjustments. The production situation is studied carefully by the officers of the wartime prices and trade board and by the officers of my department who are associated with production. Adjustments have been and are being constantly made as we find overproduction in one side of an industry and underproduction in another side. That is particularly true of lumber, where we may find that an undue amount of rough lumber is reaching the market as against finished lumber. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has spoken of trim and finish. The reason for that increase was that we found that that particular side of the industry was falling behind in the requirements, and a price adjustment ,was made to stimulate that side of the industry as against the other side.

speechtext:
Under a free market how would that be adjusted? It would be adjusted by supply and demand ordinarily, but where the demand is far in excess of supply that adjustment does not take place, and there would be further discrepancies in my opinion in a free market.
I have heard a great deal about ideologies, about the forces of freedom as against the forces of control. But it seems to me there is no principle of that kind involved in this bill. The policy of this goverment is for an orderly return to a free economy, and the bill before us is simply a measure to provide the machinery for effecting that orderly return. It seems to me that the word "freedom" is being used entirely outside its proper context. Someone, for purposes of illustration, spoke of a man falling off the deck of an ocean liner in mid-ocean. That man would have freedom of the seas, freedom to sink or

swim, but still he would not be very happy.
Freedom involves a certain price-how much can the community afford to pay for that freedom? In the case of lumber, if we decontrolled lumber today the cost of that to the people of British Columbia who buy in the retail market would be about $50 a thousand. It would be very fine to have a free market in lumber and no one would desire it more than myself, but that is a high price to charge the people of British Columbia for the privilege of buying in a free market in competition with the present export demand.
That is the case with many commodities. As I say, steel is today controlled, and it is being moved in an abnormal way to meet an abnormal demand, which is partly the result of Canada's inability to buy steel outside its own boundaries. That is a unique situation; it does not ordinarily apply. But that has been the situation for the past year and probably will be for another year. It is necessary for Canada tc get the last ounce of production from its own facilities and to control the price, which otherwise would be a runaway price. For the first time in history, I presume, steel is selling in Canada below the price of steel in the United States. The price of steel in Hamilton, is below the price of steel in Pittsburgh.

Yes; the movement from Algoma and Sydney is a subsidized price, but the price of production in Hamilton is not a subsidized price. Suppose we removed control from steel. Steel is the basis of all industrial costs; if the price of steel went up five dollars a ton every product that uses steel would rise in price, and one of the principal items would be a rise in the price of agricultural implements. We control steel in order to control a vast list of commodities against an abrupt change in price which would be entirely out of proportion to the cost to the government of control. That, I believe, is the desirable thing to do at this time. It is a thing we hope we shall not have to do for many months. We hope that there will be an easing of the world situation in steel; but, until that easing comes, it is very much in the best interests of the buyers of Canada to have steel control continued.
We are freeing commodities as fast as we can, and we do not always wait for them to get in easy supply. For example, cement was freed from control last summer when cement was a very tight commodity in this country. Why was that done? It was done because the production of cement is in a few hands, and

Emergency Powers
we were able to get the assurance of industry that removal of control would not result in price increases; that is, we were able to get that assurance with regard to many articles even though they may continue to be scarce. Of course, articles that come into free supply can be freed immediately so that the law of supply and demand may operate.
It has been said frequently that the removal of price control would play into the hands of monopolies and great corporations; but I can tell the committee from experience that there is less price fluctuation and less taking advantage of removal of control by monopolies and big corporations than there is by a great group of smaller producers. You get a more disorderly market where you have a great number of smaller producers selling on the market than you do on a market that is controlled by a small group of producers.
A great deal has been said about aluminum in this country. I may say the price of aluminum was twenty-one cents a pound at the beginning of the war; it was fifteen cents a pound at the end of the war, and it is now lli cents a pound. That is not a controlled commodity. That price is established because responsible producers believe that a lower price stimulates demand and is a wholly desirable part of their merchandising.
This government is moving to a return to a free economy as rapidly as it can. It seems to be perfect nonsense to cross-examine the government on the meaning and intent of this bill. It is a simple bill; it asks that certain regulations which have been maintained in the orders be allowed to remain for a period of not longer than another year.

The trouble with the C.C.F. position is that it seems to assume that controls will be possible indefinitely under our constitution. That is not so. We have to get back to a system of decontrol whether we want to or not. The trouble with the Tory position, if I may say so, is that they talk about this being a disorderly decontrol, and the control they advocate a more orderly decontrol. They are flying in the face of the experience of the United States, and they are flying in the face of probabilities. To listen to the speeches which were made this afternoon, one would have thought that marvellous results accrued from the decontrol in the United States; that prices went up slightly and that that stimulated a vast volume of production and that that volume of production brought prices down again. That is the theory of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, and the theory that some of these hon. gentlemen are putting forward. But it is pure theory. It was not fact. It was not the factual development. Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to provide compensation to government employees who have suffered death or disability by accident:, arising out of or in the course of employment or by reason of an industrial disease out of or in the course of employment and to the dependents of such employees; such compensation and. costs as may be awarded and the costs of administration to be paid out of the consolidated! revenue fund. With provision also empowering the Minister of Finance to require employers to pay the compensation awarded their employees together with expenses of administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR DISEASE, DISABILITY OR DEATH ARISING OTJT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the principle contained in this resolution is to recognize and extend the principle of compensation. The Government Employees Compensation Act enacted in 1918 provides for compensation to those who are injured or whose death may be caused by an accident arising out of and in the course of their employment. That act is known as chapter 30 of the revised statutes of 1927, as amended by chapter 9 of the statutes of 1931. The principle recognized therein is one which has been asserted over the years. This resolution is the forerunner of a bill which will extend the principle materially. The compensation which will be provided is that which is already provided under provincial legislation for persons other
1824	COMMONS
Compensation for Government Employees_
than employees in the service of His Majesty under the law of the province in which the accident occurs.
The liability and the amount of compensation are also provided under that legislation. Since 1922 compensation for the employees of His Majesty has been in the hands of and administered by the Department of Transport. Claims arising from accidents or otherwise are handled differently according to the provinces. I think it is safe to say that in all provinces except Quebec the application is made directly to the workmen's compensation board of the province in which the accident or death occurred. The Department of Transport, by agreement with the provincial boards, is able to deal with the accidents through the boards and to grant compensation in accordance with the schedule of tariffs set out in the provincial acts.
In Quebec the procedure is somewhat different, in that the department deals directly with the individuals, except in cases which I shall mention when we come to the bill.
The resolution extends the principle of compensation, in that it would include disabilities and deaths arising from industrial diseases.
The resolution's main features may be summarized under the following heads: (1) it continues the Government Employees Compensation Act as it now stands; (2) it provides compensation in cases of disablement by industrial disease, as I said a moment ago, according to the law of the province in which such disease is contracted; (3) it empowers the governor in council to declare employees of government companies, corporations, boards or agencies to be employees subject to the act; (4) it provides compensation for employees residing in the northwest territories in accordance with the law or ordnance of the Yukon territory; (5) it provides compensation for employees ordinarily resident in a province who are injured or disabled while performing the work in the Yukon territory or northwest territories, according to the law of the province where such employee is ordinarily resident; (6) it provides compensation for employees who are injured or disabled while employed outside Canada; (7) it empowers the governor in council to make regulations providing compensation for employees who contract pulmonary tuberculosis in government hospitals. There are several extensions of the principle of compensation as outlined in the original act, and I shall be glad to discuss them in greater detail when the bill is before the house.

That is a good explanation. I want the minister to believe that I am in support of the bill. I am just seeking the widest information that I can get.
The minister particularly mentioned industrial diseases. That is something with which I am familiar because of my many years' connection with a large industry. I have seen many men lose their lives as a result of industrial diseases, and that is what I had in mind a few moments ago when I said I was not 100 per cent satisfied with the operation of the Ontario act in that regard. I may say that many many cases have come to my attention in the last twenty-five years, cases of employees of industry who lost their lives because of industrial diseases.
I had one case brought to my attention not so long ago, that of a man whom I knew. He was a moulder ini a plant. It is not necessary to mention the name of the city or to specify the plant. He contracted a disease which caused his death. I am certain that he contracted the disease because he worked under a skylight which was unprotected. There was no glass covering between him and the skylight. In due course he died. In spite of anything I could do to obtain compensation for his wife-I was certain he died through a disease contracted from the unprotected skylight-I could make no impression on the board because they stated they had to take the decision of. the medical staff. I hope that in the bill which the minister is going to bring in, under such circumstances, if a workman in any plant over which the government has control contracts an industrial disease and the medical staff say that the disease was not contracted through his employment, he or his family will have an appeal from the medical staff. If the minister has not that in his bill, then I hope, when the bill is brought down and I bring the question up again, he will be able to assure me that the workmen will have an appeal from the medical staff. I do not think for one moment that the medical staff of any compensation board should have the last word on whether a workman has come to his death through disease contracted in a plant, if they say he has not. Doctors know a great deal, I admit, but there are some industrial diseases they do not know to the extent of 100 per cent, in any event.
I myself worked in industry for approximately a quarter of a century and, as I said a few moments ago, know of many men dying
from having contracted industrial diseases. They died from that cause, in spite of what the medical staff of the compensation board said. If I were in the Ontario house or had any connection whatever with the workmen's compensation board in Ontario, I would do my best to have the Workmen's Compensation Board Act amended to such an extent that the report of the medical staff in reference to an industrial disease would not be final until the workman or his family was allowed to appeal to a judge or a court. I would1 take the decision of the judge more readily than I would take the decision of the medical branch of the compensation board. I hope that when the minister brings his bill in he will, having in mind what I have said, be able, to assure me in any event that a workman in any government plant, or a miner, in the Northwest Territories, who contracts an industrial disease, will have a court of appeal above the medical staff of the board.
I do not know that I have much more to say about the matter tonight. I am not opposing introduction of the bill. I shall be prepared to discuss it when it does come in, and its various clauses. I have no doubt that I shall be in a position to support the bill very generally. The reference I have just made to the medical branches of compensation boards is a result of many contacts with them in contests for compensation to families of men who, I knew, died from an industrial disease. I hope that there will be some provision in this bill to give the workman an appeal above the medical branch of a board.

I desire to ask the minister before the resolution is carried, and it arises out of the wording of the resolution where it says "employees who have suffered." Does that mean that it is retroactive and will take into consideration employees' cases which are now being considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR DISEASE, DISABILITY OR DEATH ARISING OTJT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Yes. That is covered
by a section in the bill which will protect any cases which are now pending.

subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR DISEASE, DISABILITY OR DEATH ARISING OTJT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The minister mentioned
two compensation acts, the act of 1918,1 think, and the act of 1931. Is this a bill amending those acts, or is it a complete bill in itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR DISEASE, DISABILITY OR DEATH ARISING OTJT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It is a completely new
bill repealing the old acts and extending the principles contained therein.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Chevrier thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 105, respecting compensation for government employees.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow the Minister of Finance will ask for interim supply, as he has already informed the leaders of the various parties and groups in the house, and also ask that we deal with further supplementary estimates for 1946-47, which amount to approximately $55,000,000. Then we shall continue with the discussion of the bill in the name of the Minister of Transport; then second reading of Bill No. 26, also in the name of the Minister of Transport; then there is a bill in the name of the Secretary of State in regard to trading with the enemy. I think that will probably be sufficient.
Mr. MaeINNIS:	In what order will they
be taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As far as possible in
the order I have mentioned.

Will the house be sitting
tomorrow night?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. On account of
certain obligations elsewhere, I understand that the house will not sit tomorrow night.
Mr. MaeINNIS:	What are the particular
reasons why the house is not to sit tomorrow night? It seems to me that we have all the time in the world, judging from the way we are carrying on.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, March 28, 1947
